Thanks for your information. Your question is made very clear and it is an interesting and helpful issue.

As you have discovered, the invisible stem is important, because it is used as a bud to grow leaves.
However, a bud stem should be only subtype 2 stem, and it grow only the subtype 2 leaf.

I have modified your code to create the following code, which generate the following screen shot.
One bug still exist: sometimes the stem turned into leaves and sometimes there is less stem.
I don't know if it is a python parameter (nomally xml parameters are used) issue or a child node calculation issue.
Hopefully, you can just run the code multiple times to find the best outcome.

Sorry for the inconvenience, as the plant structure is truly flexible and diverse, an omini and bug-free system is hard to achieve. Just like the bud mutation still exist in plants.

For issue number 2:
you main step is of subtype 1. Thus, if you give suptype 1 as successore of that stem, you will have an infinit loop where each stem has an infinit number of creating successors which are identical to itself (because there are no growth delays as you noted, all successor-shoots get created at the same time).
To get the leaf (which is of subtype 2) as successor, you need to set in your stem:
parameter name="successor" number="1" type="2" organtype="4" percentage="1"

For backward compatibility, if you give <[...] type="2" [...]> and no organtype (ie.parameter name="successor" number="1" type="2" percentage="1"/) for the successor of a stem, cplantbox assumes that it s a leaf successor.

but it would indeed be good to have failsafe to stop that form happening

for problem 1):
now you can decide whether the growth delay in the plants (both shoot and roots) is defined, via one of 3 methods.
to define which method you wish to implement, you can add the general plant parameter:
<parameter name="delayDefinition" value="2"/>
in the seed parameter set (see [testLatDef.xml)](https://github.com/Plant-Root-Soil-Interactions-Modelling/CPlantBox/blob/master/modelparameter/structural/plant/testLatDef.xml)
the options are:
- distance based, using the growth rate and the apical zone length (value = 0)
- time-based where cplantbox uses the ldelay parameter given by the parent organ (value =1)
- time-based where cplantbox uses the ldelay parameter given by the child organ (value = 2)

if you d like to implement different method between the roots and the shoot, we can update the code (e.g. distance bsaed for the roots and time based forthe shoot).

All good now ! (see attached figure)
I'm not planning to implement different methods for root and shoot so no need to develop a specific feature (for me at least).

I think the issue might be caused by the way the time loop is defined. Indeed, the problem becomes clearer if you set 
`plant.simulate(dt=dt, verbose=True)`
The 'verbose=True' allows you to see from which age to which age the plant gets simulated.
It then becomes easier to see that you are actually doing: `finalPlantAge = tf + dt`
Which is why, when dt is larger, the stem is longer at the end of the simulation and there are more leaves.
For me it seems that setting:
`t = np.arange(start=ti, stop=tf, step=dt)` (instead of `t = np.arange(start=ti, stop=tf+dt, step=dt)`)
solved the issue

I did consider that possibility and I think it's something else because reading the documentation for numpy.arange : 

> `stop` : integer or real
End of interval. The interval **does not include** this value, except in some cases where step is not an integer and floating point round-off affects the length of out.

Which is why I added `+dt` to the `stop` argument.

When I define several time steps in a list and try them out like this: 
```
list_dt = [10, 1, 0.1, 0.01]
for dt in list_dt:
    t = np.arange(start=0, stop=30, step=dt)
    print(f'dt={dt} tmax = {max(t)}')
```

I get: 
| dt   | t max |
|------|-------|
| 10   | 20    |
| 1    | 29    |
| 0.1  | 29.9  |
| 0.01 | 29.99 |

But when I run: 
```
for dt in list_dt:
    t = np.arange(start=0, stop=30+dt, step=dt)
    print(f'dt={dt} tmax = {max(t)}')
```

I get the expected final time (the same for all simulations): 
| dt   | t max |
|------|-------|
| 10   | 30    |
| 1    | 30    |
| 0.1  | 30.0  |
| 0.01 | 30.0 |

So the simulations are actually of the same duration. 

I'll dig a little deeper with the verbose output of the `simulate()` method.

What is importnant to keep in mind is that the output of 'np.arange(start=0, stop=30+dt, step=dt)' will give you the plant age at the beginning of each time step. And you want to have an equal plant age at the end of the last time step not at the beginning of the last time step. To get the plant age at the end of the time step you need to do:
```
dt = 30
t_beg = np.arange(start=0, stop=30, step=dt)
t_end = np.arange(start=0, stop=30, step=dt) + dt
```

You were right, there was some confusion between the time vector `t` and `simulate(dt)` on my part.

is it so that the f_se (after the copy) still corresponds to se = rb.ProportionalElongation() created before the copy in python?
Yes, exactly :-) but C++ in rootsystem::simulate(double dt, double maxinc_, std::shared_ptr<ProportionalElongation> se, bool verbose)

Longer version of the answer:
it is a quick fix, and makes rootsystem::simulate(double dt, double maxinc_, std::shared_ptr<ProportionalElongation> se, bool verbose) easier.

In rootsystem::simulate we pass the ProportionalElongation, and use the organism::copy to test different scales. Therefore, it is convenient to still have the same ProportionalElongation object.

If we copy ProportionalElongation we would need to get the right ProportionalElongation reference back from the copied RootSystem to test the scales, but we would have a copy for each subType (which in inconvenient). Or, we could set the original ProportionalElongation in the new copy of the Rootsystem. So, just to not copy the ProportionalElongation seemed easier.

Dear noemiversluijs,
Thank you for reaching out and well done with adapting the script.
1) In CPlantBox, plants are made of nodes connected by segments, creating a network with no cycles. Consequently, a plant with _N_  segments will have _N+1_ nodes. `rx` is the water potential of the root system, given per node. It should be of shape [N] (with N still the number of nodes). `sx` is the mean water potential of each soil voxel, taken from the potential at the center of the voxel, it will be as long as there are voxels.  `soil_fluxes` is the plant water uptake summed per voxel (as several root segments can be in the same soil voxel), it is a dictionary where each key is the index of a cell and the values give the net plant water uptake in the voxel (voxels with no roots are not in the dictionary). the nodes array give the 3D coordinate of each nodes, it is of chape [N,3]. 
2) CPlantBox is a stochastic models. The realised value of each plant organ parameter will be taken from a normal distribution using the mean and std value given in the parameter file. Moreover, the tropism function (which sets where each new plant segment points to) is also in part random. If you want to have each time the same values, you can send a 'random seed' to the plant object. This way, the random function used within CPlantBox will give the same sequence of random number at each simulation. I added a commented line `rs.setSeed(0)`, you can uncomment it to get this fixed behavior.
3) In your script, `get_nodes` is called before the simulation loop. However, each time `rs.simulate(dt)` is called, the plant grows (unless it has reached its maximum size) and the number of nodes and segments can increase. Therefore, the size of rx obtained at the end of the simulation is longer than the number of nodes stored at the beginning of the simulation. I added in your script a line of code to fix that, and updated the other plots as well.
4) other remarks: the sanity check `r.test()` needs to be updated: it throws warnings such as `Warning: segment  3071 is not mapped, this will cause problems with coupling!`. It mean that for some segments, CPlantBox did not manage to make them fit completelly in the soil space defined (e.g., the z coordinate is at -15.02, inferior to the -15cm max depth of the soil). Contrary to what the code says, it will not cause a problem in the coupling, the root segment is considered to be outside the soil and with neither loose nor gain water. So you can ignore the warning.

While the maintainers look into the specific linker flags for the native macOS build, I have created a Docker image that pre-installs all dependencies and compiles CPlantBox in a stable Ubuntu environment. This bypasses the macOS linking issues entirely.

If you simply need to run the software, you can try pulling my image:

Bash

docker pull satraox/cplantbox-image:general
To run it:

Bash

docker run -it satraox/cplantbox-image:general
This comes with the stable_v2.1 branch pre-compiled.

Option 2: Build it yourself (Recommended for Apple Silicon) Since you are on an M1/M2 Mac, building the image locally is often better as it will generate a native arm64 Linux container (avoiding Rosetta emulation).
